abstract: Background: Motor-cortex-targeted transcranial ultrasound stimulation (tUS) can influence neural activity and motor responses, but its relationship to spontaneous behavior during sleep disruption (SD) remains unclear. Objective: To examine how repeated tUS during sustained SD relates to the temporal organization of spontaneous running and inactivity bouts. Methods: We recorded wheel activity in 36 mice for 17 days. On Days 13-17, mice in control (Ctrl) or wheel-confinement SD housing received bilateral motor-cortex-targeted tUS or sham. Another 32 mice followed the same treatment schedule and completed the retention phase of the novel object recognition test before open-field testing on Day 17. EEG/EMG recordings in 11 untreated mice characterized the SD sleep-wake phenotype. Hydrophone measurements in water and simulations using individual skull models characterized acoustic exposure. Results: During the final three dark phases, SD/tUS mice had lower activity-resumption probability (0.132 vs 0.224) and longer median inactivity bouts (3.81 vs 2.48 min) than SD/Sham mice. Both housing-by-treatment interactions were significant. Within SD, neither total rotations nor running intensity differed significantly. The mean discrimination index was higher with tUS, although the Holm-adjusted comparison was nonsignificant. SD/tUS mice spent longer in the open-field center than SD/Sham mice. Across all 32 behavioral-test mice, lower resumption probability and longer pauses correlated with longer center time the next day. Untreated SD mice slept more and had more frequent sleep-wake transitions. Conclusions: During ongoing SD, mice receiving repeated motor-cortex-targeted tUS were less likely than sham-treated mice to resume wheel running. Their longer pauses between runs may provide opportunities for sustained rest.
